learning_objective: 🎭 Step into the magical world of theatre! Learn about stage types, spatial awareness, and the foundational elements of a live performance.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Theatre is a collaborative performing art that uses live performers to present the experience of a real or imagined event before a live audience in a specific place.
There are different stage setups: 'Proscenium' (picture-frame stage, audience on one side), 'Thrust' (audience on three sides), and 'Arena' or Theatre-in-the-round (audience on all four sides).

The stage is divided into zones to help actors navigate. 'Downstage' is closest to the audience, 'Upstage' is furthest back. 'Stage Right' and 'Stage Left' are from the actor's perspective facing the audience.

Blocking is the precise staging of actors to facilitate the performance of a play. It ensures everyone can be seen, prevents actors from bumping into each other, and creates visually interesting stage pictures.
The 'Set' creates the physical environment (walls, furniture). 'Props' (Properties) are the movable items actors interact with (like a letter, a sword, or a teacup) to make the scene realistic.

fun_activity.title: 🗺️ Map Your Stage
fun_activity.instructions: Clear a space in your room. Imagine the TV or window is your 'Audience'. Stand in the middle. Walk 'Downstage Center', then move to 'Upstage Left'. Understanding these terms is the first rule of acting!

exam_tips: 📌 Remember that 'Stage Right' and 'Stage Left' are ALWAYS based on the actor's point of view when looking at the audience.
📌 'Upstage' got its name because historical stages were raked (tilted upwards at the back) so the audience could see the actors in the back.
📌 Explain how different stage types (like Arena vs. Proscenium) change the connection between actors and the audience.
quick_recap: ⭐ The 'Wings' are the offstage areas to the sides of the acting area.
⭐ Theatre requires collaboration among actors, directors, set designers, and the audience.
⭐ Good blocking helps tell the story visually even if the audience cannot hear the words.
